This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is the Director of an ML research project (`schema_semantic_constrained_ie`), directing a Paper Agent to prepare the EMNLP 2026 paper "OntoCoDec" for submission. This session covers four Director instructions executed sequentially:
   
   - **D061 (completion)**: Incorporate WikiEvents EE fine-tuning composability results into the paper + retract D059 limitation
   - **Pre-submission Polish**: Clean orphan bib entries, check caption self-containedness, verify page count, check ARR checklist requirements, final em-dash scan
   - **P0+P1 Claim Upgrade**: Strengthen CF tradeoff narrative (severity distinction, root cause, EE vs RE CF, 70B CF explanation), upgrade 70B DR=0% prominence, upgrade FT composability contribution
   - **Page Compression**: Compress main body from 10 pages to 8 pages using three strategies (Related Work→Appendix, Violation Landscape compression, Method micro-compression)

   Communication protocol: Paper Agent's plain text is invisible to Director; all reporting done via `paper_agent_post_to_director` MCP tool.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **OntoCoDec**: Two-layer constrained decoding (grammar + semantic) for IE
   - **DR vs CF severity**: DR = hard constraint (triple ontologically invalid), CF = soft preference (each triple individually valid, but entity has different types across triples)
   - **CF root cause**: 100% introduced by semantic layer (grammar-only CF ≈ 0.08%)
   - **EE CF > RE CF**: EE multi-argument event structures increase entity reuse across slots
   - **70B CF baseline**: Low unconstrained CF (0.07%) reflects under-measurement (malformed outputs bypass checker), not genuine consistency
   - **Constraint tightness (κ)**: SciERC κ̄=0.333, DocRED κ̄=0.842
   - **FT composability**: RE: DR≤0.20%, R-F1±0.6pp; EE: RoV→0%, AC≤0.8%
   - **70B DR=0%**: Only configuration to completely eliminate DR on DocRED (998 docs)
   - **EMNLP 2026 ARR**: Long paper limit 8 pages main body (excl. references, appendix, limitations)

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section5_wikievents_draft.tex`** (D061 + P0.3)
     - EE FT composability paragraph added (L65-70), replacing template block

     ```latex
     % exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
     \paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
     LoRA fine-tuning extends composability to EE (20-document test set).
     Unconstrained FT models retain substantial RoV (Qwen 38.31\%, Llama 8.8\%) and AC violations (2.68\%, 3.5\%); adding S1 eliminates RoV for both models and reduces AC to $\leq$\,0.8\% (Qwen 0\%, Llama 0.8\%).
     Argument F1 remains within $\pm$1.1\,pp (Qwen 7.85$\to$8.18, Llama 9.98$\to$8.91); trigger F1 shows a larger shift ($-$5.4\,pp Qwen, $-$0.6\,pp Llama), though both metrics carry wide confidence intervals at this sample size.
     The violation-elimination pattern replicates RE composability (\S\ref{sec:composability}): FT reduces but does not eliminate schema violations; S1 removes residual RoV and AC.
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/main.tex`** (Multiple edits)
     - D061: Deleted D059 limitation paragraph; updated L72 composability scope to include WikiEvents ("SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents"); updated Ethics Statement to include WikiEvents
     - Page compression: Removed `\subsection{Violation Landscape}` header
     - Current Limitations L72: `Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; EE: RoV$\to$0\%, AC$\leq$0.8\%), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA)`

     - External linter change: L13 changed from "up to 12% in zero-shot" → "up to 12% on RE and 21% on EE in zero-shot, resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning on RE"

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section7_conclusion_compressed.tex`** (D061 + P0)

     ```latex
     OntoCoDec compiles IE ontology schemas into composable token-level decoding constraints that compose losslessly with standard fine-tuning across both RE and EE: DR reaches $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp on RE (R-F1 40--46), RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE, and beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four RE violation types under fine-tuned decoding for calibrated models (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
     ```

     \section{Related Work}
     \label{sec:related_work}
     
     We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec.
     Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql,ugare2024syncode,park2024grammar,beurer-kellner2024domino,jsonschemabench2025} guarantees format validity but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints; type-constrained code generation~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022,scholak2021picard,pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compiles type systems into token-level masks but operates on static type declarations, whereas IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation.
     Vocabulary-constrained IE methods~\cite{geng2023gcd,sainz2024gollie,josifoski2022genie,guidex2025,vukovic2024dore,boostcd2025} restrict which tokens can appear but not which type combinations are valid per relation; EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires supervised training and hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
     Training-based methods~\cite{paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,lu2022uie,knowcoder_acl2024,li2023codeie,schema_rl2025} provide soft guidance; post-hoc approaches~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} validate outputs after generation.
     OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, is training-free, and compiles constraints automatically from ontology schemas.
     Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,grammar_aligned_2024,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026,dccd2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.

     Baseline DR violations are 15.37\% (SciERC) and 18.46\% (DocRED), comparable rates driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology scale (\S\ref{sec:introduction}); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate) predicts the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops from 0.08--10.21\% (zero-shot) to $\leq$\,0.20\% (LoRA), and CF from 2.57--12.02\% to $\leq$\,1.18\%, while R-F1 remains within $\pm$0.6\,pp (\S\ref{sec:composability}).
Under fine-tuning, the grammar layer becomes a no-op and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\%.

% §5 Setup (compressed from Violation Landscape)
% exp_ids: mvp_phase0_violation_rate, mvp_phase0_scierc_schema,
%          mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred, mvp_phase0_docred_schema

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR violations are 15.37\% (SciERC) and 18.46\% (DocRED), comparable rates driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology scale (\S\ref{sec:introduction}); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec.
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql,ugare2024syncode,park2024grammar,beurer-kellner2024domino,jsonschemabench2025} guarantees format validity but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints; type-constrained code generation~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022,scholak2021picard,pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compiles type systems into token-level masks but operates on static type declarations, whereas IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation.
Vocabulary-constrained IE methods~\cite{geng2023gcd,sainz2024gollie,josifoski2022genie,guidex2025,vukovic2024dore,boostcd2025} restrict which tokens can appear but not which type combinations are valid per relation; EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires supervised training and hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
Training-based methods~\cite{paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,lu2022uie,knowcoder_acl2024,li2023codeie,schema_rl2025} provide soft guidance; post-hoc approaches~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} validate outputs after generation.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, is training-free, and compiles constraints automatically from ontology schemas.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,grammar_aligned_2024,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026,dccd2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.

% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$); constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
Grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%; Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), confirming that CF is introduced by the semantic layer's per-slot type enforcement, not by grammar constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), which establishes the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, which supports orthogonal composability.
Post-fine-tuning, grammar is a no-op; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\% (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}).
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates residual DR and reduces CF to $<$1\% for both Qwen and Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

8	\label{sec:wikievents}
9	
10	To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
11	The framework requires no modification: grammar compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned type constraints via the same registry.
12	Violations extend to Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), and Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR).

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that enforce structural and type-validity constraints during autoregressive generation:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (virtually eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} that enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
%
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), with 1--2\% persisting even after fine-tuning; rates are driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology or model scale.
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp of unconstrained baselines (R-F1 40--46): near-lossless composability at deployment-grade extraction quality.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Under zero-shot decoding, which stress-tests constraint robustness at low extraction quality (R-F1 2--8\%), DR drops by 42--99\% across three model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) with no significant F1 cost (DocRED: $+$0.50\,pp, $p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
With beam search ($k{=}4$), the full stack eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) while preserving extraction quality (R-F1 44.23 and 46.11, respectively); in zero-shot beam decoding, DR reaches 0\% for calibrated models on both RE datasets.
The framework generalizes to event extraction (WikiEvents: 56 event types, 80 roles) without architectural modification and eliminates event-vocabulary and role-vocabulary violations ($\to$ 0\%); where unconstrained outputs are severely off-schema, format compliance additionally enables entity extraction (Entity F1: 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).
Fine-tuning composability extends to EE: LoRA + S1 eliminates RoV and reduces AC to $\leq$\,0.8\% on WikiEvents.
Per-slot enforcement introduces a cross-field consistency trade-off (up to 12\% on RE and 21\% on EE in zero-shot, resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning on RE).

The framework bridges the gap between flexible generative extraction and the type-safety requirements of downstream knowledge systems.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Constraint enforcement matters most at deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%): at this level, residual type violations propagate directly into knowledge graphs and decision-support pipelines; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning, OntoCoDec reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46); under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), which stress-tests constraint robustness, DR drops by 94\% on SciERC while remaining F1-neutral.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA fine-tuning across RE and EE (three datasets, two 8B-class model families): DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46) on RE; RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE. Zero-shot robustness across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and three datasets: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); WikiEvents vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\% (Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%); 70B achieves DR$\to$0\% on both RE datasets.
    \item Characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent in per-slot enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) and reduces DR to 0\% for calibrated models in zero-shot settings.
\end{enumerate}

38	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
39	\label{sec:grammar}
40	
41	The grammar layer compiles $\mathcal{O}$ into a context-free grammar (CFG) enforced at every decoding step via logit masking.
42	This compilation proceeds in two stages.
43	
44	\paragraph{Schema-to-grammar compilation.}
45	We generate a JSON Schema encoding the structure in Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints restricting entity types to $\mathcal{E}$ and relation types to $\mathcal{R}$.
46	This schema is compiled into an EBNF grammar via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, producing a pushdown automaton tracking JSON structure and enum membership.
47	
48	\paragraph{Logit masking.}
49	At step $t$, the automaton computes grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$; all others receive logits $-\infty$.
50	This simultaneously enforces: (i)~structural validity (well-formed JSON), (ii)~relation vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$), and (iii)~entity type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$).
51	Domain/range constraints are \emph{not} enforced, as they depend on entity types within each triple; this gap is filled by the semantic layer.
52	
53	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
54	\label{sec:semantic}
55	
56	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
57	
58	\subsubsection{Entity Registry}
59	\label{sec:entity-registry}
60	
61	As the model generates the entity list, the semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ mapping each entity to its declared type.
62	This registry is populated incrementally: when the model completes an entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$, the pair $(n_i, \tau_i)$ is added to $\mathcal{D}$.
63	The registry is then consulted during relation generation to look up the declared types of head and tail entities.
64	
65	\subsubsection{Position Detection}
66	\label{sec:position-detection}
67	
68	At each step $t$, the processor pattern-matches the decoded prefix to identify the current field position; semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
69	
70	\subsubsection{Dynamic Masking}
71	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
72	
73	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$ restricting generation to type-valid tokens.
74	
75	\paragraph{Head type masking.}
76	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
77	If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
78	Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
79	If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.
80	
81	\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
82	At a \textsc{TailType} position, the head type $\tau^h_j$ is already determined from the decoded prefix.
83	The processor computes $\operatorname{range}(r_j, \tau^h_j)$, the valid tail types conditioned on the generated head type (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).
84	If $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when it belongs to this set.
85	This sequential check ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) achieves exact pair-based enforcement, strictly tighter than an independent range check $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r)$.
86	
87	\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
88	Each type name $\tau \in \mathcal{E}$ must be mapped to token IDs for logit masking.
89	A naive approach maps $\tau$ to its first subword token and sets disallowed IDs to $-\infty$, but this fails in two scenarios:
90	(1)~SentencePiece tokenizers produce context-dependent tokenizations where the same string yields different token IDs depending on preceding context (e.g., after a JSON delimiter), and
91	(2)~ontologies with prefix-shared type names (e.g., \textsc{Sen}, \textsc{Sid}, \textsc{Side} in WikiEvents) map to the same first token, making single-token disambiguation impossible.
92	We resolve both with \emph{continuation masking}: at compile time, we scan the full vocabulary to build a prefix map identifying, for each type name, all tokens whose decoded text is a valid prefix.
93	At decode time, the semantic mask allows any token that continues a partially-generated type name, disambiguating over multiple steps.
94	This is tokenizer-agnostic, handling byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral) without tokenizer-specific logic.
95	
96	\subsubsection{Grammar-Semantic Interaction}
97	\label{sec:interaction}
98	
99	The final mask is the conjunction of $G(t)$ and $S(t)$, permitting only tokens satisfying both layers.
100	This embodies an \emph{enabling dependency}: semantic lookup requires relation types to be valid members of $\mathcal{R}$, guaranteed only by the grammar layer; without it, semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\%.
101	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$, the system falls back to grammar-only control (\emph{grammar-first fallback}), preserving structural validity at the cost of a potential type violation.
102	Formal analysis of composition, fallback behavior, and constraint tightness is in \S\ref{sec:composition}.
103	
104	
105	\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
106	\label{sec:strategies}
107	
108	\paragraph{S1: Single-pass decoding.}
109	Both constraint layers are active throughout a single generation pass.
110	The entity registry is populated as entities are generated and immediately available for relation-level type checking.
111	This is the simpler and recommended strategy. It achieves strong constraint enforcement with higher relation F1 than the two-pass alternative.
112	
113	\paragraph{S2: Two-pass decoding.}\label{sec:s2}
114	A first pass extracts entities under grammar constraints; extracted entities compile an input-dependent grammar for the second pass, which generates relations under both grammar and semantic constraints.
115	S1 achieves higher R-F1 at comparable DR (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}) and is the primary configuration.

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate) predicts the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops from 0.08--10.21\% (zero-shot) to $\leq$\,0.20\% (LoRA), and CF from 2.57--12.02\% to $\leq$\,1.18\%, while R-F1 remains within $\pm$0.6\,pp (\S\ref{sec:composability}).
Under fine-tuning, the grammar layer becomes a no-op and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\%.

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
Zero-shot decoding stress-tests constraint enforcement at low extraction quality (R-F1 2--8\%).
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$); constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small

Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
Zero-shot decoding stress-tests constraint enforcement at low extraction quality (R-F1 2--8\%).
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$); constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
Grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%; Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), confirming that CF is introduced by the semantic layer's per-slot type enforcement, not by grammar constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), which establishes the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,

% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small

& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\

\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\

  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\

  & 9.90

$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
Full S1 reduces DR from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while R-F1 is unchanged (8.23\,$\to$\,8.36, $p{=}0.58$).
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\%, reaching 0\% on 4/7 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
Post-hoc filtering achieves slightly higher F1 via precision gains but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
CF rises from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
Grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%; Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), confirming that CF is introduced by the semantic layer's per-slot type enforcement, not by grammar constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), which establishes the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}

%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).

CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates residual DR and reduces CF to $<$1\% for both Qwen and Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

Grammar-only eliminates RV and ET with no F1 impact while DR remains at 14.84\%, the ceiling of grammar-based decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}; grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%), confirming CF originates from the semantic layer.

\subsection{Cross-Task Validation: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
The framework requires no modification: grammar compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned type constraints via the same registry.
Violations extend to Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), and Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: WikiEvents three-model comparison (v3 final)
%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.8pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Mode}
  & EV\,$\downarrow$ & RoV\,$\downarrow$ & AC & CF
  & Trig.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Unconstr.\ & 24.0 & 74.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 11.8 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 76.1 & 8.2 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 2.1 & 21.1 & 13.4 & 14.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 10.5 & 88.8 & 0.1 & 0 & 5.7 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 77.0 & 8.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 3.8 & 17.2 & 7.5 & 17.6 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Mistral\\7B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 37.3 & 63.9 & 0 & 0 & 2.4 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 64.0 & 13.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 1.3 & 14.9 & 3.9 & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{WikiEvents EE results (246 documents, zero-shot).
Violation rates over parsed documents.
---: not applicable (grammar-only has no semantic-layer metrics).
F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:wikievents}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV exceeding 85\% combined; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), and all models yield entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot identify well-formed mentions in off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), which validates tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
Grammar-only ablation isolates each layer: grammar eliminates EV ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at 64--77\% because the CFG cannot constrain 80 argument roles conditioned on event context; AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\%, the same latent-violation surfacing pattern observed in DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}).
Full S1 then drives RoV to 0\%, which demonstrates layer complementarity.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to confusion between semantically similar entity types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN) where grammar-first fallback permits the incorrect type.
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument event structures increase entity reuse across slots: a single entity may fill roles in multiple events, each imposing different type constraints through per-slot enforcement.

Post-hoc filtering is impractical for EE: it retains only 23/5{,}467 arguments for Qwen (99.6\% discarded), 3/5{,}053 for Llama, and 0/6{,}034 for Mistral, because unconstrained models generate generic role names rather than ontology-specific ones.
Unlike RE, where constraints are F1-neutral, EE shows measurable gains: entity F1 rises from 0\% to 11.7--17.6\% and trigger F1 increases by $+$1.5--1.8\,pp, because grammar enforcement produces schema-valid JSON that the parser can process.

% exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
LoRA fine-tuning extends composability to EE (20-document test set).
Unconstrained FT models retain substantial RoV (Qwen 38.31\%, Llama 8.8\%) and AC violations (2.68\%, 3.5\%); adding S1 eliminates RoV for both models and reduces AC to $\leq$\,0.8\% (Qwen 0\%, Llama 0.8\%).
Argument F1 remains within $\pm$1.1\,pp (Qwen 7.85$\to$8.18, Llama 9.98$\to$8.91); trigger F1 shows a larger shift ($-$5.4\,pp Qwen, $-$0.6\,pp Llama), though both metrics carry wide confidence intervals at this sample size.
The violation-elimination pattern replicates RE composability (\S\ref{sec:composability}): FT reduces but does not eliminate schema violations; S1 removes residual RoV and AC.

\paragraph{Cross-scale generalizability.}
\label{sec:70b-results}
-To evaluate cross-scale generalizability, we test OntoCoDec on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4 quantization).
-On SciERC, the 70B model produces fewer baseline violations than its 8B counterpart (DR 6.5\% vs.\ 13.3\%), yet violations persist; OntoCoDec eliminates them entirely (DR$\to$0\%, R-F1 $-$0.03\,pp).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Constraint enforcement matters most at deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%): at this level, residual type violations propagate directly into knowledge graphs and decision-support pipelines; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning, OntoCoDec reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46); under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), which stress-tests constraint robustness, DR drops by 94\% on SciERC while remaining F1-neutral.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA fine-tuning across RE and EE (three datasets, two 8B-class model families): DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46) on RE; RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE. Zero-shot robustness across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and three datasets: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); WikiEvents vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\% (Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%); 70B achieves DR$\to$0\% on both RE datasets.
    \item Characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent in per-slot enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) and reduces DR to 0\% for calibrated models in zero-shot settings.
\end{enumerate}

Zero-shot robustness across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and three datasets: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); WikiEvents vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\% (Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%); 70B achieves DR$\to$0\% on both RE datasets.

-    \item Characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent in per-slot enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) and reduces DR to 0\% for calibrated models in zero-shot settings.
+\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]

+    \item A systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE: rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology scale, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.

+    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer framework compiling ontology schemas into stateful logit masks that enforce pair-based domain/range constraints during autoregressive IE, unlike code generation where types are statically declared.

+    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA across RE and EE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost on RE, RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE. Zero-shot robustness across four models (8B--70B) and three datasets: DR $\downarrow$42--99\%, WikiEvents violations $\to$0\%; 70B achieves DR$\to$0\% on both RE datasets.

+    \item Analysis of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off in per-slot enforcement (resolved to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\% by fine-tuning); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned decoding.
\end{enumerate}

shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning (Banerjee et al., 2025; Park et al., 2024b; Schall
and de Melo, 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Reddy et al.,
2026); however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints (Tam et al., 2024), and OntoCoDec
constrains only type tokens while leaving entity
spans unconstrained.

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontology schemas into
composable token-level decoding constraints that
compose losslessly with standard fine-tuning across
both RE and EE: DR reaches ≤ 0.20% with R-F1

Limitations
CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated
models (Qwen, Llama), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02%) as a consequence of
per-relation independent enforcement; for poorlycalibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87% → 1.27%) by constraining type
assignments to schema-valid values. CF fallback
ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR (+13.85 pp). CF↔DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix C). Entity F1 impact is model-dependent (+1.22 pp for Qwen vs.
−0.64 pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1% vs. 6.8%). Zero-shot results cover three 7–8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4–8% compared to ∼45%
for fine-tuned systems. Composability with finetuned models is validated on SciERC, DocRED,
and WikiEvents with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.18B (RE: DR ≤ 0.20%, R-F1 within ±0.6 pp; EE:
RoV→0%, AC≤0.8%), but evaluation is limited
to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF
(Qwen 1.18%, Llama 0.46% on SciERC) traces
to schema-level type ambiguity (G ENERIC↔X)
rather than enforcement failure. The continuation
masking approach (§3.3) handles multi-token type
names and prefix-shared types on the ontologies
tested (6–27 entity types); scalability to ontologies
with hundreds of entity types has not been validated, and the prefix-map size may grow substantially. Global entity-level type consensus during
decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF
violations. Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8Bclass and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated only on 8B-class models. Scaling to smaller models has not been verified, and the
dual-factor pattern’s predictive scope may differ at
other scales. CF type inconsistencies may propagate to downstream tasks that consume extracted
triples (e.g., knowledge graph construction, question answering); the impact of such propagation has
not been evaluated. Residual DR under fine-tuning
(36 violations across all fine-tuned settings, both
models and both datasets) decomposes into entity
type errors (39%), schema coverage gaps (33%),
and model generation errors correctly caught by
constraints (28%); Llama DocRED alone accounts
for 33 of 36 residual violations (92%), reflect8

ing weaker entity typing (Appendix C). Schema
coverage gaps (one-third of residual violations)
are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone
(training-set frequency coverage); complementary
approaches such as global type consensus or posthoc correction may address this limitation. All
main experiments use greedy decoding; our evaluation of beam search on the full SciERC test set
(551 documents) and a DocRED subset across three
models confirms compatibility (Appendices E, F),
but comprehensive evaluation across all decoding
configurations remains future work. Evaluation is
limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA) on two
8B-class models; scaling fine-tuning to 70B-class
models, other training paradigms (full fine-tuning,
RLHF), and non-English ontologies remains to be
explored.
